plain: It's a closet on the internet where your project lives: today's files, plus every version they've been through. It works like the history of a shared document: you write over it, save, and if tomorrow you regret it, you can see how it looked on Tuesday and get it back exactly as it was. It's useful for two very specific things: keeping your work from being lost even if your computer falls down the stairs, and letting other services read that folder and turn your files into a real website, with its own address and everything. It can all be done from the page itself, dragging files with the mouse, without typing a single strange command into any black screen.

account.free: Yes, and the free plan is more than enough for the whole course: 0 dollars, no card. It includes unlimited project folders, public and private, with as many people in them as you want, full history from day one, and website publishing with GitHub Pages. The paid plans are for businesses: GitHub Pro runs about 4 dollars a month and Team about 4 dollars per person per month. The Copilot AI assistant is separate, around 10 dollars a month, with a limited free version. Check the day's figures at github.com/pricing, because they change; you don't need any of these plans.
steps: Go to github.com. Top right there's a button that says Sign up. It asks for email, password, and a username. Careful with the name: it shows up in the address of everything you publish, github.com/your-name, and changing it later breaks links. Keep it short, lowercase, no accents, no jokes; two years from now you'll be showing it to a client.

GitHub gives you a visual puzzle under the heading Verify your account and then sends you an eight-digit code by email, subject Your GitHub launch code. You have to solve that puzzle by hand: nobody and nothing can do it for you. Copy the code, paste it, and you're in.
Choose the free plan and skip the survey

On the next screen, check the Free column and click Continue for free. Then it asks what you do and what you want it for: at the very bottom there's a small link, Skip personalization. Click it and save three minutes.

Profile photo top right, Settings, left column Password and authentication, and there Two-factor authentication. GitHub requires it of almost everyone, so do it now instead of when it blocks you. When you're done, it shows you a list of recovery codes: download them and keep them wherever you keep your passport. Lose your phone without those codes and you lose the account and everything in it, with no customer support that can save you.
In Settings, Emails section, check the box Keep my email addresses private. Skip this and your real email is visible in every save you make, and spam crawlers pick it up within days.

Go back to the home page and click the green New button in the left column, or the + sign top right and New repository. A repository is simply a project's folder. Give it a name with no spaces or accents, for example my-first-project. Check Private. And also check Add a README file, because an empty repository shows a screen full of commands you're not going to use.
Find the button you're going to click a thousand times

Once inside the repository, above the file list, on the right, there's a button that says Add file. Expand it and two options show up: Create new file and Upload files. The second opens a big zone that says Drag files here to add them to your repository. That's your workspace. Try it now with any loose file to get comfortable with it.
account.warning: Anything you upload to a public repository can be read by anyone, and deleting the file afterward fixes nothing: the old version stays in the history forever. No passwords, no API keys, no .env file, no invoice PDF with your ID number on it. When in doubt, create the repository as Private: switching it to public later takes two clicks, and the other way around is a disaster. And if a key ever slips out, removing it isn't enough: go into the service that issued it and revoke it. There are bots scanning GitHub around the clock, and leaked keys get used within minutes, with bills of hundreds of dollars in your name.

first: Create a private repository named my-first-project with the Add a README file box checked. You land right inside it.
Click Add file and then Upload files. Drag in from your desktop the files the AI wrote for you. Wait for the blue bar to finish before touching anything.

Scroll down to the Commit changes box. Where it says Add files via upload, write instead what you uploaded, for example first version of the studio website. Leave Commit directly to the main branch checked and click the green Commit changes button.

Above the file list, on the right, there's a clock with an arrow and a number next to it: those are your saves. Click it. That's your full history. Open the first one and see how GitHub paints additions in green and removals in red.
With the repository open, press the period key: a full editor opens inside the browser. Look at it, close the tab, and move on. I just want you to know it exists.
shortcuts: The . (period) key, while in the repository

Opens github.dev, a full editor inside the browser, nothing to install. Same address, swapping github.com for github.dev. It's how you touch ten files in a row without forty clicks. When done: branches icon in the left bar, Source Control, type the message at the top, and click the blue Commit & Push button.
The t key, while viewing the code
File search by name. Type indx and it already offers you index.html. Same as the Go to file button above the list. Past twenty files, it's the only sane way to get around.
The e key, with a file open
Jumps straight into edit mode, same as the pencil top right. The move you'll do every day: open the file, press e, Ctrl+A to select everything, Ctrl+V to paste what the AI gave you, and save.
The y key, with a file open

Freezes the browser address to today's version. That's the link you hand to the AI or a friend so they see exactly the same code you're looking at, even if you change it tomorrow. Without this, tomorrow the link shows something else and nobody knows what you're talking about.
The b key, with a file open
Blame view (literally, blame). Tells you, line by line, which save each one showed up in and with what message. It's the answer to when did this break and what was I doing that day.
The l key, with a file open

Jumps to a line number. When the AI tells you to change line 84, press l, type 84, and you're there. You can also click a line's number and then another with Shift to mark a whole block and copy its link.
g then c, g then i, g then p
Quick jumps inside the repository: to Code, to Issues (your task list), and to Pull requests (proposed changes). Pressed one after the other, not at the same time.
The ? key
Shows the cheat sheet with every shortcut that works on the screen you're on. They change from screen to screen. When you forget one, check this before Googling it.
Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac)
GitHub's command palette. Type anything — a repository name, a file, an action — and jump straight there. If you only learn one shortcut, make it this one.
Add file button, then Upload files
Your daily bread. Opens the drag zone. You can drop loose files or whole folders, and GitHub keeps whatever folder structure they bring. Limit: 100 files per batch and 25 MB per file.
daily: Upload files by dragging: Add file, Upload files, drop them, and wait for the blue bar. If the folder has subfolders, they're kept as is. If a file with that name already exists, it gets overwritten by the new one and the old version stays in the history, which is exactly what you want.
Edit without leaving the browser: open the file, press the e key or the pencil, Ctrl+A, Ctrl+V with what the AI gave you, and save. This is 80 percent of your work here.

Write the save message as if telling someone: change the buttons' color to blue, not Update index.html. That text is the map you'll use when you want to go back. It's the one thing that separates a useful history from a pile of noise.

Check the history: the clock with the arrow above the file list shows every save on the project. And inside a file, the History button shows only that file's saves. Green is what got added, red what got removed.

Go back to an earlier version without fear: open the old save, click Browse files (see the files as of that moment), open the file, click the Raw button (raw, the content stripped bare), Ctrl+A, Ctrl+C. Go back to the current file, e key, Ctrl+A, Ctrl+V, and save with the message reverting to the March 12 version. Nothing gets deleted: you create a new save with the old content. This is the single most important thing in this guide.
Hand context to the AI: open the file, press y to freeze the link, and paste it. If the repository is private, the AI can't get in: click Raw, copy the content, and paste it in full.

Confirm it's been published: if you have Vercel connected, a little circle shows up next to the last save. Spinning orange, it's publishing. Green with a checkmark, your site is live on the internet, takes between twenty seconds and two minutes. Red with an X, it failed and your public site is still showing the previous version, which is a very nice safety net.

templates.name: README.md: the project's cover page
templates.what: The README is the file GitHub shows automatically when you open your repository, below the file list. It's for three audiences: a client who wants to understand what this is, the AI you paste the link to, and above all yourself six months from now when you've forgotten everything. It's written in Markdown, which is plain text where a hash makes a heading and a dash makes a bullet.
templates.how: If you checked Add a README file when creating the repository, you already have it: open it, press the e key, select everything with Ctrl+A, and paste this over it. If you don't have it: Add file, Create new file, type README.md into the name field (with exactly those capitals and the .md ending) and paste the content into the big box. Before saving, click the Preview tab to see it formatted instead of as raw symbols. Then fill in the brackets and click Commit changes.
fill: [PROJECT NAME]
The name you tell people, with spaces if needed. Doesn't have to match the repository's name.
[One sentence saying what it does and for whom]
What you'd tell your brother-in-law over dinner. No jargon.
[https://your-project.vercel.app]
The address Vercel gave you when you published. If you haven't published yet, write not published yet.
Table of important files
The three or four files you actually touch. The rest don't belong in that table.
Context for the AI
Colors, tone, audience, and what nobody should touch. This is what you paste to the AI every time.

There are no keys or passwords in here. Keys live in Vercel's panel, under Settings > Environment Variables.

templates.name: .gitignore: the file blacklist
templates.what: A text file that marks what should never end up published: keys, passwords, and giant folders like node_modules, which can have fifty thousand files and weigh hundreds of megabytes. It's respected by the browser editor (github.dev) and any tool that uses git underneath. Honest warning: when you drag files by hand into github.com, this list doesn't stop you, there you're the filter. Even so, having it prevents most accidents and tells the AI what's secret in your project.
templates.how: Add file, Create new file. In the name field type .gitignore, starting with the period and nothing after it; GitHub accepts that name even though it looks odd. Paste the content into the big box, check that nothing of yours is missing, and click Commit changes. From then on, in github.dev you'll see those files dimmed gray, a sign they won't be uploaded.
fill: credentials.txt / keys.txt
Swap those names for whatever you actually use to store passwords, if you have any in the project folder.
node_modules/, .next/, venv/
Leave them even if you don't know what they are. If your project doesn't have them, they do no harm.
*.mp4, *.psd
Add here any heavy file type you use: *.ai, *.wav, big *.pdf files.

templates.name: One-page website that publishes itself on Vercel
templates.what: A complete index.html, styling included, that works as is and looks good on mobile. Needs nothing installed and doesn't depend on any other website. Useful for a local shop, a studio, a freelancer, or for getting something real published on the internet in under ten minutes and losing your fear of the whole thing.
templates.how: One: in your repository, Add file, Create new file, name it index.html in lowercase, at the root, not inside any folder. Paste the code and click Commit changes. Two: go to vercel.com and click Continue with GitHub; authorize the connection when asked. Three: in Vercel's panel, click Add New then Project. Four: in the Import Git Repository list, find yours and click Import. If it doesn't show up, click the Adjust GitHub App Permissions link and grant access to that repository. Five: under Framework Preset choose Other and don't touch anything else. Six: Deploy button. Wait between twenty seconds and two minutes, confetti shows up, and an address like your-project.vercel.app. From then on, every time you click Commit changes on GitHub, Vercel republishes on its own. To roll back the published site: Deployments tab, find the one that worked, three-dot menu, and Promote to Production. On money: Vercel's Hobby plan is free, 0 dollars, but its terms prohibit commercial use; if you're going to sell or charge for that site, you need the Pro plan, around 20 dollars per person per month (check the price at vercel.com/pricing). Adding your own domain is free on Vercel, but the domain itself has to be bought separately, between 10 and 15 dollars a year depending on the ending.

templates.name: CONTEXT.md: the sheet you paste to the AI every day
templates.what: The file that solves vibecoding's most tiresome problem: every new conversation with the AI starts from zero and doesn't remember your project. You save it in the repository, and at the start of any session you open it, click Raw, copy, and paste. The AI starts off knowing what you're building, how you work, and what not to touch. Saves twenty minutes and prevents half of all disasters.
templates.how: Add file, Create new file, name it CONTEXT.md. Paste this, fill in the brackets, and click Commit changes. Every time something important about the project changes, come back, press the e key, update it, and save. Practical rule: if you've just explained the same thing to the AI for the second time, this file is missing a line.

Current status
The table of files, what works, and what's half-done. Update it when you finish something.
What NOT to touch
The most valuable part of the file. This is where you write what already works, so the AI doesn't rewrite it while chasing something else.

Colors, typography, and the rule against external libraries. Without this, every session proposes redoing everything differently.
Versions that did work
The permanent links (y key) of the good saves. It's your undo button.
templates.code:
# Project context

I paste this to the AI at the start of every conversation. Saves me twenty minutes of explaining.

## What I'm building

[One sentence. Example: a one-page website for my ceramics studio, with hours, prices, and a button to message me on WhatsApp.]

## Who it's for

[Who visits, from what device, and what they want to accomplish in under thirty seconds.]

## How I work (read this before answering me)

- I don't know how to code and I don't use the terminal.
- I upload and edit files from the github.com website, dragging or with the browser's pencil.
- It publishes itself on Vercel every time I save.
- I need COMPLETE files, no trimming, no ellipses, and no sentences like here goes your code.
- Always tell me the exact file name and which folder it goes in.

## Current status

| File | What's in it | Status |
|---|---|---|
| index.html | [what's in it] | working |
| css/style.css | [what's in it] | working |
| [file] | [what's in it] | half-done |

## What NOT to touch

[List of files or parts that already work and that I don't want to change, not even their name.]

## Decisions already made

- Colors: [paste the color codes]
- Typography: [name]
- No external libraries or anything that needs installing.
- Has to look good on mobile before it looks good on desktop.

## Next

1. [Next change]
2. [The one after]

## Versions that did work

- [date] — [what existed that day] — permanent link: [open the file and press the y key, paste the address here]

errors: Yowza, that's a big file. Try again with a file smaller than 25MB.

Dragging through the website, GitHub won't accept files over 25 MB. Almost always a video, a PSD, or unedited photos straight from the phone. Fix: that file doesn't belong in GitHub. Upload the video to YouTube or Vimeo and link it from your site; run the photos through squoosh.app or similar until they're under 300 KB, which will also make your page load fast. GitHub is for text, it's not a hard drive.
Yowza, that's a lot of files. Try again with fewer than 100 files.

You dragged in a folder with more than a hundred files at once, and 99 percent of the time the culprit is node_modules, a folder the AI generates that can hold tens of thousands of files. Don't upload it: it's useless in GitHub and regenerates on its own. Remove that folder from what you're dragging in and upload the rest. If your project genuinely has over a hundred files of its own, upload them in batches: one folder, save, then another.
The repository [name] already exists on this account.

You already have another repository with that name. The warning shows up in red below the name field as soon as you finish typing (the exact wording may vary slightly by website version). Give it a different name, for example adding -v2 or the year. And take the chance to open the existing one: it might be the same project you started three weeks ago and forgot about.
Push cannot contain secrets — Secret scanning found a [key type] on line X

GitHub has detected what looks like an API key inside the file you were about to save and blocked the save. It's doing you a huge favor. Do this, in this order: one, go to the service that issued that key (OpenAI, Stripe, Supabase, whatever it is) and revoke or regenerate it, because a secret is considered burned the moment it leaves your computer. Two, remove the key from the file and keep it out of the code. Three, if the key is genuinely needed for the site to work, it goes in Vercel: Settings, Environment Variables, and that's where it's kept safe. Never use the link to bypass the warning.
This branch has conflicts that must be resolved

Conflict: two versions of the same file touched the same line and GitHub doesn't know which one to keep. Usually happens if you edit from your phone and your computer without reloading, or if you have github.dev open in an old tab. Click the Resolve conflicts button: you'll see the file with some odd symbols, less-than signs, equal signs, and greater-than signs, separating the two versions. Delete the symbols and keep the text you want. Once none are left, click Mark as resolved and then Commit merge. If it overwhelms you, copy the whole text and ask the AI to hand you back the clean file.
404 — This is not the web page you are looking for.

The page doesn't exist. Three causes, in order of frequency: the repository is private and you're not signed in, or you signed in with a different account; you got a letter wrong in the name, and GitHub is case-sensitive; or you deleted or renamed the file and the link points to the old spot. Check top right which account you're signed in with. If you sent the link to someone and it works for you but not them, the repository is private: share the content via the Raw button or make it public deliberately.
Error: No Output Directory named "public" found after the Build completed.

This shows up on Vercel, not GitHub. Vercel looked for a folder with the result and didn't find it, because it thinks your project is a type it isn't. Fix: on Vercel, go into the project, Settings, Build and Deployment, Framework Settings section; set Framework Preset to Other and leave Output Directory empty, with the Override switch off. Then, Deployments tab, three dots on the last one, Redeploy. If your project genuinely uses something like Vite or Next.js, tell the AI which framework you use and have it give you the exact value for that field.

Vercel published, but when you visit it, it can't find the home page. Almost certain cause: your file isn't named exactly index.html, or it's tucked inside a folder instead of at the repository's root. GitHub is case-sensitive: Index.html and index.html aren't the same. Go into the repository, check that index.html shows up on the first screen, not inside anything. If it's in a subfolder, open it, e key, copy everything, create a new file named index.html at the root, and paste. Republish and try again.

prompts.name: Have the AI hand you the project ready to drag into GitHub
prompts.prompt: Act as the trusted engineer for someone who doesn't know how to code. I'm not going to open any terminal or install anything: I work only from the github.com website, dragging files and editing with the browser's pencil, and I publish on Vercel. I'm building [DESCRIBE YOUR PROJECT IN ONE SENTENCE: for example, a one-page website for my yoga studio, with hours, prices, and a contact button]. I want the whole project, ready to upload today. Rules you can't skip. One: give me the exact list of files and folders, with the name written exactly as it should be, lowercase, no accents, no spaces, and tell me which goes at the root and which inside a folder. Two: give me the complete content of each file, one by one, in separate blocks, without abbreviating, without ellipses, and without phrases like your content would go here. Three: the start file has to be called index.html and be at the root. Four: don't put any key, password, or token inside the files; if the project needs one, tell me separately and explain where it actually gets stored. Five: nothing over 25 MB and no folder with more than a hundred files, because the GitHub website won't let me upload them. Six: use [PLAIN HTML AND CSS, IF YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT ELSE TO PUT] and avoid any external library that needs installing. Finish by telling me in what order to upload the files and what I should see on screen if it's working.

prompts.name: Go back to the version that worked, without breaking anything
prompts.prompt: I have a project on GitHub and I've broken it. I don't know how to code and I work only from the website, no terminal, editing files with the browser's pencil. I'm giving you three things. First, the file exactly as it is right now: [PASTE THE COMPLETE CONTENT HERE, OR THE PERMANENT LINK YOU GET BY OPENING THE FILE ON GITHUB AND PRESSING THE Y KEY]. Second, the message and date of the last save when it did work: [PASTE THE COMMIT MESSAGE AND DATE, AND IF YOU CAN, ALSO THAT OLD VERSION'S CONTENT]. Third, what I'm seeing now that's wrong: [DESCRIBE THE EXACT SYMPTOM: blank screen, the button does nothing, red text shows up, the published site doesn't load, it looks bad on mobile]. I want you to do four things, in this order and without mixing them up. One: compare the two versions and tell me in plain English what changed and which of those changes is suspect number one, with a sentence of why. Two: give me the complete file content as it should be to work again, whole and in one piece, so I can select it all and paste it over. Three: write me the exact message I put in the Commit changes box so that three months from now I understand what I did. Four: tell me how I confirm in two minutes that it's fixed. Don't explain any git commands or ask me to install anything.

prompts.name: Fix a failing Vercel deployment
prompts.prompt: I work without a terminal, everything from the website. I have a GitHub repository called [REPOSITORY NAME], with [DESCRIBE WHAT'S INSIDE: for example, an index.html at the root, a css folder, and an img folder], connected to Vercel to publish itself. The last deployment came out red. I'm pasting you the full log that shows up when I open the failed deployment and click Build Logs: [PASTE THE ENTIRE LOG TEXT HERE, FROM THE FIRST LINE TO THE LAST, EVEN IF IT LOOKS LONG]. In Settings, Build and Deployment, I have Framework Preset set to [WHATEVER IT SAYS: Other, Next.js, Vite, or another], Build Command set to [WHATEVER IT SAYS OR THE WORD EMPTY], and Output Directory set to [WHATEVER IT SAYS OR THE WORD EMPTY]. Answer me in this order. One: point me to which line of the log is the one that actually matters, copy it, and translate it into plain English, no jargon. Two: if it's fixed by changing a setting in Vercel, tell me the exact name of the field, which screen it's on, and what value to type. Three: if it's fixed by changing or adding a file in the repository, give me that whole file and its exact name, and tell me which folder it goes in. Four: how do I trigger the publish again from the website without touching the code. Five: how do I go back to the previous version that was published, in case this makes things worse. No terminal commands at any point.

prompts.name: Check you're not about to publish anything secret
prompts.prompt: I'm going to upload these files to a GitHub repository that will be [PUBLIC OR PRIVATE] and I can't tell what's dangerous to publish. I'm pasting the content of the files, one after another, with its name before each one: [PASTE THE FILES HERE]. Review them as if you were my business's security officer and give me a list of everything that shouldn't leave my computer: API keys, tokens, passwords, database connection strings, personal emails, phone numbers, account numbers, paths that include my Windows username, internal addresses, and anything that could be used to spend money in my name. For each finding, give me four things: which file and which line it's in, which service issued it, what a stranger could do with it, and how much it could cost me in dollars in the worst case. Then give me two things ready to copy and paste: the complete content of a .gitignore file adapted to this specific project, and the corrected version of each affected file, with the secret replaced by an empty placeholder and a note of where that real value should go. Finally, explain in numbered steps, with no terminal, how I revoke from the website each key that may have already leaked, service by service, with the name of the menu where it's done. If you find nothing dangerous, say so clearly and don't invent findings to look good.

words: Repository (repo)
A project's folder inside GitHub, with all its files and all its past. One project, one repository.
Commit

A named save. It's not like Word's Ctrl+S, which overwrites what was there before: here every save stays forever in the list and you can go back to any of them. On the website it's the green Commit changes button.
Branch
A copy of the project for trying things out without touching the good one. Working solo you don't need it: stay on the main one.
main
The name of the main branch, the real one, the one that gets published. When GitHub asks, always leave Commit directly to the main branch checked.
README
The file GitHub shows automatically when you open your repository. The cover page. Written in Markdown and ends in .md.
Markdown (.md)
Plain text with three rules: a hash for headings, a dash for bullets, and two asterisks around a word to bold it. That's it.
.gitignore
The list of files that should never get uploaded: keys and giant folders. The dot at the start is part of the name.
Raw
The button that shows a file stripped bare, without GitHub's decoration. It's what you copy to paste to the AI or to recover an old version.
Deploy
Taking the files and turning them into a live website, with its own address. It's what Vercel does on its own every time you save.
Pull request
A proposed change for someone else to review before accepting it. It exists, works very well, and you won't need it while working solo.
matters: The message on every save. Writing change the buttons' color to blue costs four seconds; writing Update index.html costs zero. The difference gets paid the day something breaks and you have two hundred identical entries in the history: without useful messages there's no way to know which version to go back to, and you end up guessing blindly or redoing the work.

Public or private, and what's inside. A public repository is read by the whole planet, bots included, and those bots hunt for API keys around the clock. A leaked OpenAI or Stripe key gets used within minutes and the bill lands on your card: there are documented cases of hundreds of dollars in one night. And deleting the file doesn't remove it from the history. Default to private, and if a key slips out, revoke it at the service before doing anything else.

The two-factor authentication recovery codes. Ten digits GitHub shows you once, and almost everyone closes the window without saving them. Lose your phone without them and there's no phone number to call: you lose the account, the project, and the published site, all at once. Keep them in your password manager or printed in a drawer.

Save small and often. One change, one save. Upload forty files at once and the site stops working, you have forty suspects and no lead. Upload three at a time and you know exactly which one broke it and go back in a minute. It's the difference between a quiet afternoon and a long night.
ignore: The whole terminal side: git clone, git push, git pull, SSH keys, and those black boxes full of commands that show up in every tutorial. There's another path and it's the one you're using. When a tutorial starts with open the terminal, close the tab and look for how to do it from the website.

Branches, pull requests, merges, and code reviews. Those are for teams. Working solo, always stay on main and save directly: you skip half the concepts and lose absolutely no safety, because the history covers you just the same.

The whole social and automation showcase: GitHub Actions, Issues, Projects, Wiki, Discussions, the stars, the followers, and the pretty profile with colorful graphs. None of that makes your project work. Come back to it once you have three projects published and running.
